title: Protein and vitamin B12 in nutritional yeast

seo.title: Nutritional yeast: protein and vitamin B12 explained
seo.meta_description: Nutritional yeast is protein-dense, but B12 depends on fortification. NIH lists 8.3–24 mcg B12 per roughly 1/4 cup among several fortified brands.
seo.search_intent: Understand how much protein and vitamin B12 nutritional yeast provides and why fortification matters

excerpt: Nutritional yeast is protein-dense, but vitamin B12 should never be assumed from the product name alone. A USDA survey reference provides about 40.4 g protein per 100 g, roughly 4 g in a 10 g serving. For B12, NIH lists several fortified brands at about 8.3–24 mcg per roughly 1/4 cup, while unfortified products may provide no reliable B12. Check the Nutrition Facts label every time.
content_html:
Two claims about nutritional yeast often travel together: it is high in protein, and it supplies vitamin B12. The protein can be an inherent feature of dried yeast; the B12 is often there because the manufacturer fortified the product.

Protein is concentrated, but serving size still matters

A current USDA survey reference provides about 40.4 g protein per 100 g. At a 10 g serving, that is roughly 4.0 g protein. Fifteen grams would provide about 6.1 g if the product matched that reference.

That can make a useful contribution to a meal, but a dusting of flakes does not automatically become the meal's main protein source.

B12 is the part you must verify

Vitamin B12 occurs naturally mainly in animal-derived foods. NIH notes that plant foods do not naturally contain B12 unless fortified. Nutritional yeast can be an excellent fortified source, but only when B12 has actually been added.

NIH lists fortified nutritional yeast from several brands at about 8.3–24 mcg of vitamin B12 per roughly 1/4 cup. The U.S. Daily Value for adults and children age 4 and older is 2.4 mcg, so some fortified products provide several times the Daily Value in a serving.

Why the range is so wide

Fortification is a formulation choice, not a fixed property of the yeast. One manufacturer may add a modest amount of cyanocobalamin or methylcobalamin; another may add much more; an unfortified product may have no dependable B12 at all.

That is why an online average is a poor way to dose B12. The current label is the relevant number.

Can nutritional yeast be a B12 source in a vegan diet?

Yes—if it is fortified and eaten in a quantity that reliably supplies the intended amount. Because formulations can change, people relying on it for B12 should recheck the label when they change brands or when packaging is updated.

Protein and B12 should be evaluated separately

A high-protein unfortified nutritional yeast can be nutritionally useful while contributing no reliable B12. A fortified product can supply substantial B12 in a small serving. These are two independent features.

The simplest shopping rule is therefore: use grams per serving to judge protein, and the explicit B12 line on the Nutrition Facts panel to judge vitamin B12.

faq.question: How much protein is in nutritional yeast?
faq.answer: The USDA survey reference used here contains about 40.4 g/100 g, roughly 4 g in 10 g.

faq.question: Does all nutritional yeast have B12?
faq.answer: No. B12 commonly comes from fortification, and unfortified products may not be a reliable source.

faq.question: How much B12 is in fortified nutritional yeast?
faq.answer: NIH lists several fortified brands at about 8.3–24 mcg per roughly 1/4 cup, but the exact amount depends on the product.

faq.question: Can vegans use nutritional yeast as a B12 source?
faq.answer: Yes if the product is fortified and the label confirms a reliable amount per serving.
